lesson.title: Sound and image

steps.headline: Alliteration repeats a consonant sound, and assonance repeats a vowel sound.

lead.text: Alliteration repeats a consonant sound at the start of nearby words, usually on stressed syllables. Assonance repeats a vowel sound inside nearby stressed syllables, whatever the consonants. Both belong to sound, not spelling: “cider” and “sorrow” alliterate, “cider” and “cat” do not.
Sonnet 30 opens: “When to the sessions of sweet silent thought”. Say it aloud and listen to how each word begins.

reveal.text: Three words share the opening sound: sessions, sweet and silent. The hushed s suits a line about silent thought. Keats opens “To Autumn” with “mists and mellow”, two m sounds that slow the line.

lead.text: Assonance follows the sound of a vowel, whatever the spelling. Say each word aloud.

reveal.text: The long vowel of “bride” returns in “qui-”, binding the urn's two names together. Shakespeare's “new wail my dear time's waste” sounds the vowel of “wail” again in “waste”.

steps.headline: Count the long i sounds in Keats's “Thou still unravish'd bride of quietness”.

workedSteps.text: The model word is “bride”, with the long vowel of “time”.
“Still” and “unravish'd” have the short vowel of “sit”, so they do not match.
Count the words with the long vowel of “bride”, the model word included.

model.source: Keats, 'Ode on a Grecian Urn', line 1

steps.headline: A simile compares openly, and a metaphor identifies one thing with another.

lead.text: A simile compares with “like” or “as”: the word keeps the two things apart. A metaphor asserts that one thing is another, with no such word. Then it can build on the assertion, as in “The classroom was a zoo”.
Burns writes “O my Luve's like a red, red rose.” Look for the word that tells you how the comparison is made.

reveal.text: “Like” keeps the two things apart: his love resembles a rose. Romeo does something stronger with “Juliet is the sun”. He asserts it, then tells the “fair sun” to “kill the envious moon”.

spans.text: But soft, what light through yonder window breaks?

lead.text: I. A. Richards called the subject of a metaphor its tenor and the borrowed image its vehicle. Dickinson's tenor is hope. She leaves the vehicle unnamed at first, so “feathers” and “perches” imply it.

reveal.text: The details add up to one creature, and the second stanza names it. Naming tenor and vehicle lets you say exactly what a figure carries across.

spans.text: Hope is the thing with feathers

model.source: Wordsworth, 'I wandered lonely as a Cloud'

spans.text: That floats on high o'er Vales and Hills,

lesson.orientation: Hear alliteration and assonance. Tell a metaphor from a simile and name the tenor and vehicle of a figure.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh text after a delay.

blocks.text: A tongue-twister is hard to say because its words keep opening with the same sound.

intro.promise: By the end you'll hear alliteration and assonance, and tell a simile from a metaphor by its tenor and vehicle.

recap.keyIdea: Poets repeat sounds and borrow pictures. Alliteration and assonance work on the ear, and a simile or metaphor carries a tenor across in a vehicle.

blocks.text: You found three s sounds in Sonnet 30 and two long i sounds in Keats. You also marked Burns's “like” and read the bird behind Dickinson's hope.

recap.nextHook: Sounds and pictures fit into forms. Next: the sonnet, its rhyme scheme and its turn.

questions.prompt: In 'When to the sessions of sweet silent thought', how many words begin with the s sound?
hints: Read the line aloud and listen to how each word begins.
Ignore s sounds in the middle or at the end of words.
Check the nouns and adjectives one by one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three: 'sessions', 'sweet' and 'silent'. The hushed s sounds suit a line about silent thought.

questions.onCorrect: Three: “sessions”, “sweet” and “silent”. The hushed s sounds suit a line about silent thought.

misconceptions.feedback: “Sessions” begins with the same sound as “sweet”. Check each word again.
Count only words that begin with the sound. Sounds in the middle or at the end do not count.
Read the line aloud: more than one word begins with that sound.

questions.prompt: In Keats's 'Thou still unravish'd bride of quietness', how many words contain the long vowel heard in 'bride'?
hints: Listen to vowel sounds rather than letters: 'still' has a short vowel.
Say 'quietness' slowly: qui-et-ness.
Count every word whose vowel matches the one in the model word, including that word itself.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: 'bride' and 'quietness' (qui-). 'Still' and 'unravish'd' have the short vowel of 'sit'.

questions.onCorrect: Two: “bride” and “quietness”. “Still” and “unravish'd” have the short vowel of “sit”.

misconceptions.feedback: Listen to vowels, not letters. “Still” has the short vowel of “sit”.
“Bride” itself counts, and one more word shares that vowel.
Count only words that match the vowel in the model word.

questions.prompt: Burns: 'O my Luve's like a red, red rose.' The comparison is made with 'like'. Name the figure.
hints: The figure announces itself as a comparison; its name shares a root with 'similar'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A simile: an explicit comparison using 'like' or 'as'.

questions.onCorrect: A simile: the word “like” announces the comparison.

misconceptions.feedback: A metaphor identifies one thing with another outright. Look for the word that announces the comparison here.

questions.prompt: In Dickinson's 'Hope is the thing with feathers / That perches in the soul', hope is pictured as a creature. Which creature is implied?
hints: It has feathers and perches, and in the next lines it sings.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A bird: the feathers, the perching and later the singing belong to it, and the second stanza names 'the little bird'.

questions.onCorrect: A bird. The feathers and the perching fit it, and the second stanza names “the little bird”.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the details in the lines: it has feathers, perches and sings. The second stanza names the creature plainly.
Feathers belong to a different kind of creature. Check the details the lines give.

questions.prompt: Wordsworth: 'I wandered lonely as a Cloud.' Name the figure.
hints: Look for the word that announces a comparison.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A simile: 'as' makes the comparison between the speaker and the cloud explicit.

questions.onCorrect: A simile: “as” makes the comparison between the speaker and the cloud explicit.

misconceptions.feedback: A metaphor would say he was a cloud. Look for the word that announces the comparison.

questions.prompt: Romeo: 'It is the east, and Juliet is the sun!' Which statement is accurate?
hints: Is there a 'like' or an 'as'?

acceptedIdeas: It is a metaphor: Juliet is identified with the sun
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A metaphor: Romeo identifies Juliet with the sun rather than comparing her with 'like' or 'as'.

choices.label: It is a metaphor: Juliet is identified with the sun
It is a simile, because two things are compared
It is alliteration on the s sound

questions.onCorrect: A metaphor: Romeo identifies Juliet with the sun rather than comparing her with “like” or “as”.

misconceptions.feedback: There is no “like” or “as” to announce a comparison, so the identification is made outright.
The s sound does repeat, but the question is about how Juliet and the sun are related.

questions.prompt: Say “Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers.” How many words begin with the p sound?
hints: Say it aloud and listen to how each word begins.
Ignore the small words in between.
Count the words that start with the p sound.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Six: Peter, Piper, picked, peck, pickled and peppers.

questions.onCorrect: Six. The same sound opening nearby words is what the ear picks up as a pattern.

misconceptions.feedback: Check each word again. One more begins with the same sound.
Count only words that begin with the sound. “Of” and “a” do not.
Listen to every word that opens with the sound, not just the first few.

questions.prompt: How many of these pairs alliterate: knee and nose; cat and city; phone and fish?
hints: Say each pair aloud.
Listen for the first sound, not the first letter.
“Phone” and “fish” begin the same way, but check the others.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: knee and nose share the n sound, and phone and fish share the f sound. Cat and city start with k and s.

questions.onCorrect: Two. Alliteration follows sound, not spelling: knee and nose match, and so do phone and fish.

misconceptions.feedback: Say each pair aloud. Spelling can mislead you in both directions.
Say “cat” and “city” aloud. Do they begin with the same sound?
Listen to the first sound of each word, not its first letter.

questions.prompt: Which word marks the comparison in “Her voice was like honey”?
hints: Which small word says that two things are being compared?
questions.onCorrect: “Like” announces the comparison. That makes it a simile, and without it the line would be a metaphor.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the thing she is compared with. Find the small word that announces the comparison.
That is what is being described. Find the word that announces the comparison.

questions.prompt: In Wordsworth's “I wandered lonely as a Cloud”, which is the vehicle?
hints: Which word names the thing borrowed to make a picture?
questions.onCorrect: The vehicle is the borrowed image. The cloud carries a picture of drifting alone.

misconceptions.feedback: The speaker is what is being described. The vehicle is the image borrowed to describe him.
“Lonely” is the quality the two share. The vehicle is the thing borrowed for the picture.
